repos.title: World-in-Context: Interactive Video World Modeling with In-Context Conditioning
repos.paper_summary: World-in-Context is an interactive video world modeling framework that conditions a flow-matching video backbone on view, action, and camera controls by placing them as tokens in the shared self-attention sequence, rather than through separate AdaLN or cross-attention pathways. Explicit discrete view tokens (Free, Fpp, Tpp) separate regime-dependent motion and enable in-video view switching. Action tokens (discrete keys and continuous increments) and Plücker-encoded camera tokens are trained jointly. Interaction-Transport RoPE (IT-RoPE) adds a zero-initialized, view-gated correction to temporal attention based on accumulated action and camera transport operators. The model is built on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B and trained on 100K navigation clips plus 500 switching sequences. On the WBench Navigation split, it scores 81.5 average, matching the 22B EchoWM (81.6) and exceeding the 5B baselines except Zing-0.5 (81.0). On the Fpp↔Tpp perspective-switching suite it reaches 93.8% success, against 18.8% for the best 5B baseline. A controlled comparison reports that joint action-camera training gives the highest rotation accuracy (90.6) and geometric consistency (90.8). Limitations: the training set is small and the paper does not report training-data statistics for the compared methods, so cross-method data-scale comparisons are omitted; the switching gain is measured on one suite.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Interactive world models need explicit view modes and separate action and camera controls, which current pipelines leave implicit or conflated.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior interactive models leave view implicit and rely mostly on camera trajectories, and this work extends in-context conditioning to them.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminary: Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: Existing models inject controls through condition-specific pathways, while the paper recasts them as condition tokens concatenated with visual latents.

digest_headlines.heading: World-in-Context
digest_headlines.headline: Explicit view tokens separate free-camera and first-person motion, and view switching emerges from single-view training.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: World-in-Context-5B nearly matches the 22B EchoWM on navigation and reaches 93.8% perspective-switching success, versus 18.8% for the best 5B baseline.

digest_headlines.heading: Applicability of World-in-Context
digest_headlines.headline: A causal variant reaches 81.2 navigation and 90.6% perspective-switching success, and the method also extends to game controls.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Positioning
digest_headlines.headline: The paper states its training set is modest and that its focus is algorithmic formulation rather than a full system or scaling study.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists data sources, quality filters, control annotation, two-stage training schedule, positional-encoding details and evaluation protocols.

repos.title: PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?
repos.paper_summary: PaperScorer is a family of supervised models that predict a paper's accept or reject decision from its content alone, using either extracted markdown text or page screenshots. Training uses anonymized ICLR submissions from OpenReview and arXiv ML papers labeled by conference proceedings, both balanced 50/50. The vision variant, PaperScorer-Vision, reaches 68% accuracy on ICLR and 77% on arXiv, improving over the best frontier baseline by 2.7% and 9.0% respectively. Its acceptance score ranks accepted papers above rejected ones, and after calibration on validation data its confidence matches test accuracy. Accuracy is highest for the lowest and highest rated papers and near chance for intermediate ratings. Screenshots retain figures and layout that text extraction discards. Limitations: the model gives no explanation for its predictions, the signal on 2026 papers is weaker because of thin data, and the impact correlation (ρ≈.25) comes from a single conference year.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Paper text alone carries recoverable accept/reject signal, but final decisions are noisy and the signal is limited.

digest_headlines.heading: Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: The task is framed as predicting the final decision from the post-rebuttal paper, with a Bayesian ceiling estimate.

digest_headlines.heading: PaperScorer: Dataset and Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Balanced ICLR and arXiv corpora were built with anonymization and shortcut controls, and training uses balanced labels.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: PaperScorer-Vision outperforms frontier baselines, and vision beats text on both datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Where does this signal lie?
digest_headlines.headline: Confidence is calibrated, but accuracy is high only at the rating extremes and concentrated in confident predictions.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work includes paper outcome prediction and reviewer agents, and this work targets label leakage in datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Applications
digest_headlines.headline: PaperScorer gives a calibrated acceptance prior that improves literature retrieval and agentic reviewing.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Causal claims, explanation, and performance on the newest papers remain unresolved limitations.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers the Bayesian ceiling derivation, data curation and shortcut audits, and edit-based perturbation analyses.

repos.title: Can Discrete Tokens Serve as Semantically Lossless Representations of Visual Signals?
repos.paper_summary: Factorized Vector Quantization (FVQ) is a multi-codebook discrete tokenizer for visual features. It applies $L$ fixed dense tight-frame projections to each visual feature, then quantizes each view with an independent codebook in parallel. The authors argue that quantization error does not determine semantic fidelity, and that the effective bit budget $L\log_2 C$ does. On a 1.7B-scale setup, FVQ keeps improving at larger budgets where residual VQ (RVQ) and product quantization (PQ) saturate, and reaches the average of the continuous QwenViT baseline. For the main model (Qwen3-8B with a 16-codebook FVQ tokenizer on Qwen3 ViT), trained on industrial-scale data, the nine-metric average is 22.8% above UniAR and 59.2% above Emu3-Chat. The paper reports competitiveness with Qwen3-VL, including on fine-grained OCR. Evidence comes from ablations on MathVista, RealWorldQA, MMStar, OCRBench, TextVQA, AI2D, ChartQA, and DocVQA. One limitation: the bit-budget claim rests on a single codebook size (C=16,384) and a single backbone family.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Discrete visual tokens may reach continuous-level understanding at large bit budgets, motivating Factorized Vector Quantization.

digest_headlines.heading: What Determines the Semantics of Discrete Visual Representations?
digest_headlines.headline: Reconstruction error does not determine multimodal understanding, and existing residual and product quantizers saturate as the bit budget grows.

digest_headlines.heading: From Bit-Budget Scaling to Quantizer Design
digest_headlines.headline: Factorized Vector Quantization gives each codebook a fixed-dimensional dense view and recovers the feature exactly before quantization.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Under identical settings, FVQ with 16 codebooks reaches 65.3 average against 64.6 for continuous QwenViT on eight benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Results support discrete tokens as a scalable interface for native multimodal models, with FVQ offered as one approach to saturation.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers the quantizer training loss, the FVQ derivation, related work, training settings, quantization-position ablation, and qualitative examples.

repos.title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution
repos.paper_summary: TraceTrial-Bench is a benchmark that treats the agent harness, the layer that connects a model to its tools, state, and lifecycle controls, as the system under test. It contains 95 tasks across seven reliability components: context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. Each task pairs a harness requirement with an agent deliverable and an external ground-truth check. A trajectory tracing module converts each harness's native logs into a shared event schema, and an evidence module selects bounded records for an LLM judge. Agent and harness layers are scored separately, each as a pass rate, and combined into a 0 to 100 score. Across 4 harnesses, 9 models, and 3,420 runs, macro-averaged harness scores range from 59.8% to 72.0%. In 31.1% of runs, the agent succeeded despite failing at least one harness criterion. Limitations: an LLM judge scores semantic criteria; activated failure-attribution links show only that predeclared endpoints and conditions matched, not that a failure propagated; and confirming a harness defect requires manual validation.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Outcome-only benchmarks give limited insight into harness mechanisms, so the paper proposes separate harness evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: An agent is a model plus a harness, and harness reliability is judged separately from whether the task succeeds.

digest_headlines.heading: TraceTrial-Bench
digest_headlines.headline: The benchmark scores agent and harness layers separately, then links failed harness criteria to agent failures via predeclared mechanism chains.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Four harnesses, nine models, and 95 tasks form a full matrix of 3,420 cells, each with one selected execution.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Claude Code leads task success at 44.0% while OpenClaw leads harness macro at 72.0%, so the two rankings differ.

repos.title: SeMo3D: Unifying 3D Generation, Editing, and Completion via Selective Modeling
repos.paper_summary: SeMo3D is a 3D diffusion model that handles generation, editing, and completion with one network by synthesizing only a selected region of a structured latent representation and leaving the rest unchanged. Training uses region-selective denoising, which applies noise and loss to randomly chosen regions of standard 3D assets, so no paired editing or completion data is needed. The architecture, Omni3DiT, is a diffusion transformer that accepts image, text, and sparse point conditions. The model is finetuned from Trellis2 at 512 resolution on Trellis-500K. On Toys4K generation, SeMo3D reports LPIPS 0.079, FID 4.99, DINO 0.926, and CD 0.0118, compared with 0.111, 5.05, 0.908, and 0.0330 for Trellis2, the image-only baseline. The provided text does not include the editing and completion tables, so this summary reports no numbers for those tasks. The paper states two limitations: the structured latent resolution cannot capture very thin structures, and the CLIP text encoder struggles with complex compositional prompts.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing 3D generation, editing and completion methods regenerate whole assets, causing task isolation, altered unchanged regions and reliance on paired data.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Editing and completion methods depend on large paired datasets, and no surveyed generator jointly uses image, text and point guidance.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: The method denoises only selected latent tokens, trains on random regions of standard 3D assets, and conditions on image, text and points.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On three benchmarks, SeMo3D ranks first on most metrics for generation, editing and completion against per-task baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Stated limits are coarse structured latent resolution, which misses thin palm fronds, and a text encoder that struggles with compositional prompts.

digest_headlines.heading: LLM Usage Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The statement lists uses of artificial intelligence tools for writing, code, feedback and experiments, with the authors fully responsible.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers training details, benchmark and metric definitions, inference settings, agent procedures, mask and point sensitivity tests, and extra results.

repos.title: AB-Attention: Accurate Block Attention for Accelerating Video Diffusion Transformers
repos.paper_summary: AB-Attention is a training-free sparse attention method for video diffusion transformers that estimates dense attention from a sample of key/value blocks instead of truncating to a top-k set. An Intra-Block Clustering Selector clusters queries only within each query block to score key/value blocks. Sampling with Inclusion-Probability Weighting draws blocks in proportion to these scores and weights each by 1/π, so one block-sparse pass gives an unbiased estimate of the attention numerator and softmax normalizer. A fused kernel packs sampled 4-token key/value blocks into full tensor-core tiles. On Wan2.1 and HunyuanVideo, the method skips 89.16% and 92.35% of attention, respectively, while baselines (RadialAttention, SVG2, DFSAttn) skip 73.63–81.03% on Wan2.1-1.3B. On Wan2.1-1.3B, AB-Attention reaches 34.4 dB PSNR against 30.0 dB for SVG2 and 2.01× speedup. The reported speedups range from 1.84× to 2.23× end-to-end on a single H20 GPU. Limitations: the kernel supports only forward inference on H20 GPUs, and evaluation covers three text-to-video models.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Dynamic block-sparse attention loses fidelity at high sparsity, and AB-Attention is proposed as a training-free fix.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Dense attention and block-sparse attention are defined as the baseline for the proposed method.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: AB-Attention scores blocks with intra-block query clusters, then samples and reweights them to estimate dense attention.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: AB-Attention gives the highest fidelity and speedup on three models, and its ablations show each component matters.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior sparse attention methods are grouped into static, dynamic, and correction-based designs, with AB-Attention positioned against them.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: AB-Attention is a training-free sparse attention method, limited to H20 GPUs, forward inference, and three models.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the sampling and estimator derivations, model configurations, baseline settings, latency protocol, and the block-size sweep table.

repos.title: EgoHSI3R: Online 4D Hand-Scene Interaction Reconstruction from Egocentric Video
repos.paper_summary: EgoHSI3R is an online, feed-forward model that jointly reconstructs camera motion, dense scene pointmaps, world-space bilateral MANO hands, and per-vertex hand contact from monocular egocentric video, without test-time optimization. It builds on the CUT3R recurrent scene model and the WiLoR hand estimator. A Hand Prompt Builder fuses WiLoR hand tokens with RoIAlign-pooled local scene features through a gate, and an Interaction-Aware Contact Builder lets MANO vertex queries attend to scene context to predict contact. On ARCTIC world-space evaluation, it reaches W-MPJPE of 108.80 mm and WA-MPJPE of 25.82 mm, improving W-MPJPE by 15.79 mm over StableHand, the strongest baseline. Its AccEr is 16.91 m/s², worse than StableHand's 4.67 m/s². In camera-space evaluation, the penalty-free variant has the best PA-p on ARCTIC (7.025 mm) and HOT3D (6.312 mm), but the standard setting's temporal jitter (13.938 on ARCTIC) is higher than dedicated smoothing methods. Limitations stated or implied: higher acceleration error, higher jitter, and the penalty-free numbers measure only matched predictions, so they do not reflect performance on all visible hands.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing egocentric methods recover hands or scene separately, so the paper targets online joint hand-scene reconstruction.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers camera-frame or world-space hands, feed-forward scene models, and contact estimation, but not all four jointly.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A recurrent scene state accumulates geometry over frames, with hand prompts and vertex contact queries feeding back into hand estimates.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments show lowest world-space hand error on ARCTIC at 108.80 mm, with mixed camera-space and contact results.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that jointly modeling hands, scene and contact in one recurrent representation gives the reported benefit.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists a capability comparison, dataset supervision and splits, efficiency measurements, loss definitions, and two extra qualitative figures.

repos.title: CuPIQP: A Batched and Differentiable QP Solver on GPUs for Robot Learning and Control
repos.paper_summary:
cuPIQP is a batched, differentiable QP solver for GPUs, built on the proximal interior-point method of PIQP. It solves many QPs concurrently and handles dense, sparse, and multistage (optimal control) structures through one interface. Each instance keeps its own iterate, parameters, and status on the device, and the shared loop stops when all instances are inactive. Dense problems use a Schur complement system with batched Cholesky. Sparse problems use augmented-system LDL factorization through cuDSS. Multistage problems use a parallel block-tridiagonal solver. Gradients come from implicit differentiation with one adjoint solve. The backward pass refactorizes the KKT system instead of storing factors, which reduces memory use at the cost of extra computation.

On benchmarks with batches of up to 16384 QPs, solve-time speedups reach 18.8× over Moreau and 4.26× over eight-core PIQP. In an end-to-end differentiable quadrotor MPC task, training is 4.6× faster than QPAX and 7.8× faster than Moreau.

The paper states two limitations. The sparse backend still needs a host-side check between iterations because of cuDSS constraints. For the IK and WBC benchmarks at the largest batch size, the paper marks cases where at least one QP fails to converge within the iteration limit.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing QP solvers target single-problem latency, so batched learning workloads need a GPU-native batched solver.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries: Proximal Interior-Point Method for A Single QP
digest_headlines.headline: Each iteration solves a Newton system from a proximal interior-point method, using a Mehrotra predictor-corrector step.

digest_headlines.heading: Differentiation through QPs
digest_headlines.headline: Gradients follow from implicit differentiation, with one adjoint solve that reuses the forward iteration matrix.

digest_headlines.heading: Batched GPU Execution and Implementation
digest_headlines.headline: Iteration control stays on the device, and workspaces and factorization structure are reused across solves.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental results
digest_headlines.headline: On batched robot QP benchmarks, cuPIQP-sparse reaches speedups of up to 18.8× over Moreau.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: cuPIQP is a batched differentiable GPU QP solver for dense, sparse and multistage problems, with nonlinear model predictive control as future work.

repos.title: DexSuite: An All-in-One Framework for Dexterous Manipulation Across Arms, Hands, and Tasks
repos.paper_summary: DexSuite is a simulation framework built on the Genesis simulator for dexterous manipulation. It provides 30 tasks, 10 arms, and 12 end-effectors that combine into more than 100 single-arm robots and thousands of bimanual pairs. The framework adds a standardized Gymnasium-compatible API, integrated teleoperation, and simulated FlexiTac tactile sensing. Workspace-aware sampling sets object placement to each arm's reachable bounding box. The authors define a benchmark of 16 task-embodiment pairs across two tracks: five tasks run with both a parallel-jaw gripper and an Allegro hand, and six run with dexterous hands only. They release 4,700 successful episodes from human teleoperation (700), scripted experts (1,200), and learned policies (2,800). Baselines include behavior cloning (state and image inputs), BC-GMM, BC-T, Diffusion Policy, and ACT. Per the paper, the dexterous hand matches or outperforms the gripper on several shared tasks. Stack and precise tool use remain hard: Stack success is at most 16% for the gripper, and Diffusion (state) reaches 9% on Allegro. Success rates are means over three seeds with 50 episodes each. The paper gives no real-robot validation, so results are simulation-only.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: DexSuite offers a simulation framework, benchmark, and dataset for studying dexterous hands against grippers.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing simulators and datasets rarely compare dexterous hands and grippers on identical tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: DexSuite
digest_headlines.headline: DexSuite adds modular robot composition, workspace-aware sampling, tactile sensing, and teleoperation on Genesis.

digest_headlines.heading: Benchmark & Dataset
digest_headlines.headline: The benchmark pairs 11 tasks in two tracks into 16 task-embodiment pairs, with 4,700 released episodes.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments and Results
digest_headlines.headline: Baselines reach 89% on Move Pan but at most 16% on Stack, with embodiment effects depending on task and policy.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A hand matches or beats a gripper on several shared tasks, but precise tool use and sequential manipulation stay hard.

repos.title: EvoTeam: Multi-Agent Collaboration via Evolving Teams
repos.paper_summary:
EvoTeam is a framework for LLM-based multi-agent systems that jointly evolves team organization, team-specific interaction rules, and individual agent skills from execution experience. It keeps a library of reusable teams: for each query, an LLM Team Selector either picks a compatible existing team or an LLM Composer creates a provisional one. A Chairman recruits a task-specific subset of the team's roster and assigns subtasks, and agents consult the team's interaction rules. After execution, reflectors update the team roster, the team's rules, and each agent's skills. Interaction rules stay within their team, while skills are reused across teams.

Evaluated on GAIA, LoCoBench (Feature and Refactor), LOCA-Bench, and BeyondSWE, with GPT-5.6-Luna as the default backbone and avg@3 scoring, EvoTeam reaches an average of 58.85 under individual-benchmark evolution, the best of the listed methods, versus 58.30 for Meta-Team. Under mixed-benchmark evolution it reaches 59.58, versus 55.55 for Meta-Team. Cross-backbone tests with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash show gains over the unevolved MAS baseline in all six configurations, up to 18.00 points on GAIA.

Limitations: the paper does not evaluate multimodal environments, and it keeps LLM parameters fixed, so the benefit depends on the base model applying stored guidance.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Improving individual agents does not reliably improve team collaboration, so EvoTeam evolves teams, interaction rules, and skills jointly.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminary Study
digest_headlines.headline: Reusing experience across heterogeneous tasks underperforms target-only evolution, traced to rigid team templates and inappropriate rule reuse.

digest_headlines.heading: The Framework of EvoTeam
digest_headlines.headline: EvoTeam selects or creates task-appropriate teams, coordinates them with team-scoped rules, and evolves teams, rules, and skills.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: EvoTeam scores 58.85 average under individual-benchmark evolution and 59.58 under mixed-benchmark evolution, the highest in each.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers individual agent evolution and collaborative multi-agent evolution, with EvoTeam targeting the latter.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: EvoTeam averages 59.58 under mixed-benchmark evolution, versus 55.55 for the strongest baseline, with transfer and ablation support.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Evaluation omits multimodal interactive settings, and results depend on the base model applying stored guidance.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethical Considerations
digest_headlines.headline: Persistent experience may retain sensitive trace data, so reused rules and skills need review and human oversight.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the algorithm, benchmark and metric details, baselines, prompts, questions and answers, and case studies.
